A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FreeCG and retain matching core methods, benchmark tables and theoretical analyses. Their text, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results on MD17, rMD17, MD22 and QM9, together with component ablations and efficiency measurements.

after.justification: v4 retains these experiments and adds periodic-system evaluations, molecular dynamics simulations, Chignolin analyses and experiments adapting FreeCG modules to QuinNet.

M1.justification: The abstract-edge, group-CG, sparse-path, shuffling and attention-enhancement pipeline remains intact. v4 adds a scalar-only MLP output-head alternative alongside the equivariant head (Appendix A.2), and explicitly incorporates FreeCG modules into QuinNet (Section 4.5). These extend the model variants without replacing the central method.

E1.justification: v4 adds Water-1k and LiPS under periodic boundary conditions, MD17 trajectory simulations, and prediction/dynamics across Chignolin conformations; v1 used Chignolin only for efficiency benchmarking. Actual QM9 evaluation also expands from six to twelve property targets in Table 4.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the retained benchmark tables are unchanged. ForceNet newly participates in the Water-1k and LiPS comparisons in Figures 8–9, alongside previously represented method families. Extending the existing QM9 comparator set to additional properties is not itself a baseline change.

E3.justification: v4 introduces substantial new evaluation protocols: 300 ps MD17 simulations at 500 K with 0.5 fs steps, periodic simulations with 200,000 steps of 0.25 fs, and a 1,000-epoch QuinNet comparison evaluated every 200 epochs. Table 5 also reverses the reported 8/32-group assignments in the staged ablation; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, shuffling and efficiency analyses, v4 tests trajectory stability through RMSD, structural-distribution recovery through interatomic-distance distributions and RDFs, performance across Chignolin conformations, and transfer of the modules to another architecture (Figures 5–6 and 8–11). These substantially broaden validation of practical behavior and generality.

E5.justification: Figure 5(c) newly reports Chignolin RMSD averaged over ten trajectories with a shaded standard-deviation band. v1 contains no corresponding repeated-trajectory uncertainty reporting. This addition is localized; the principal benchmark MAE tables still provide no uncertainty estimates or training-seed counts.

E6.justification: v4 adds six QM9 result rows, periodic-system results, simulation findings, Chignolin comparisons and QuinNet learning curves. Figures 8–9 report FreeCG force MAEs of 0.7 and 1.2 meV/angstrom on Water-1k and LiPS. Retained MD17/rMD17 numbers are unchanged, but Table 3 changes Ac-Ala3-NHMe energy MAE from 0.507 to 0.0507, and Table 5 swaps results assigned to 8 and 32 groups.

T1.justification: The composition statement around Equations 3–4 is corrected from G-equivariant to G-invariant, with the arbitrary design identified as h-prime. The force equation also gains the missing negative-gradient sign (v1 Equation 21; v4 Equation 22). The abstract-edge invariance proof and CG complexity analysis are otherwise retained.

C1.justification: The central claims about freeing CG design, the three principal components and benchmark competitiveness remain. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion add explicit claims of practical molecular dynamics applicability and successful enhancement of QuinNet, extending the earlier benchmark-focused and prospective design-paradigm claims.

C2.justification: v4 interprets the new trajectory and distribution analyses as evidence of practical simulation capability and stability. It also reverses the ablation recommendation from a small number of groups to a large number (v1 experiments; v4 Section 4.4). The original mechanism explanations largely remain, without a substantive new limitations discussion.

D1.justification: Existing implementation and hardware descriptions largely move into Appendix A. New reproducibility information includes Water-1k, LiPS and Chignolin hyperparameters, simulation settings, output-head alternatives and an EMA rate of 0.999. Conversely, v1's direct dataset-access links disappear. Both versions only promise future code release, and v4's Table 7 still lists eight groups despite Table 5 favoring 32.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantive positioning around two methodological families: geometric-vector/angle methods and irreps/CG methods. Its dedicated related-work discussion explains relationships to NequIP, Allegro, Equiformer and MACE more extensively than v1's introductory background. TensorNet, ForceNet, simulation-benchmark and water-model references are added, while several general application and classical-method references are removed.

P1.justification: The Results/Discussion/Methods organization becomes Related Works/Methods/Experiments/Conclusion, with implementation, dataset descriptions and proofs moved to Appendix A. The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten, experiments receive a clearer subsection structure, and terminology is revised, including self-attention to cross-attention.

P2.justification: The document changes from a predominantly two-column Springer layout to a single-column format with figures integrated into the narrative. Figure 1 loses its two conceptual panels while retaining the architecture panels; Figure 3 gains an explanatory grouping annotation. Tables 4 and 7 expand, and Figures 5–11 add substantial new visual evidence.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens practical validation through trajectory, distribution and Chignolin analyses, and tests the previously prospective architecture-transfer claim through QuinNet experiments. Broader QM9 reporting and mathematical corrections also improve completeness and correctness. Removed dataset links and the unresolved 32-versus-8-group discrepancy weaken reproducibility, but the new evidence addressing simulation usefulness and method generality provides a substantial net improvement.
